objects.text: What could go wrong, and what rules should my company set?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 9 of 12
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome to Session 9. For eight sessions you have built and tested things. Today we ask what could go wrong and what rules your company should set. Start with your question from last time: if this automation made a mistake tomorrow, who would be hurt first?

Keep that answer in mind, because it is the first risk you score today. You leave with a risk register for your own task and a first draft of your AI-use policy.

Here is what you leave with. A risk register for your own task, with every risk scored, owned and matched to a control. A first draft of your company AI-use policy, built from the template. And a plain view of the rules that apply in Uganda, with the names of the frameworks you will hear in meetings.

The legal part is short, and I will say clearly where you need your lawyer.

title.text: Your two hours: 45 minutes are your own work

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_88739a5f.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: 45 of the 120 minutes are yours: a register and a policy draft for your own company.

slides.notes:
The session has three big parts. Twenty-five minutes of ideas: risk scores, the four responses, the frameworks and the law. Twenty minutes on a live demonstration of how bias can enter a CV screen. After the break, forty-five minutes are yours: the register first, then the policy draft.

The last ten minutes are for your decision on your top three risks.

runs.text: 1.  Where does the secret key live, and why?
2.  Which two numbers go in your result line?
3.  Name two limits to know before you run a script.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 8. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. Where does the secret key live, and why? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. In Script Properties. A key in the code is a password on the wall: copies and screenshots carry it.

Question two. Which two numbers go in your result line? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. Minutes saved per run and errors found, both taken from the test log.

Question three. Name two limits to know before you run a script. Think about your own task as you answer.

A good answer is this. Gmail recipients a day (100 consumer, 1,500 Workspace); 6 minutes per run; a free Gemini key takes fake or sample data only.

If an answer was missing, your own task card or last workbook page has it. Now to today.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Risk register. A table of what could go wrong, how likely, how bad, who owns it and what you do about it.

Score. Likelihood from 1 to 5 times impact from 1 to 5. High is 15 or more, Medium is 8 to 14, Low is below 8.

Control. A real action that lowers a risk, such as a named reviewer or a spending limit.

Personal data. Any information that identifies a living person, such as a name with a phone number.

Shadow AI. Staff using AI tools through personal accounts, outside any company rule.

title.text:
Eight risks have followed
us through Sessions 1 to 8

rows.text: What it looks like at Nile Valley Foods
An invoice total or a quote is invented.
A price list pasted into a free chat tool.
A supplier email hides an instruction.
An automation can read the whole mailbox.
A loop calls a paid service all night.
A CV screen favours some names or places.
Data cannot be moved out of one product.
Only one person knows how the script works.

slides.notes:
Here are the risks we have met since Session 1, with one example from Nile Valley Foods for each. Wrong answers. Data leaving the company. Prompt injection, where an incoming email hides an instruction. Permissions that are too wide. Cost runaway from a loop. Bias. Vendor lock-in. And key people leaving with the only knowledge.

You will recognise most of them from your own build. Before we go on, tell me which one worries you most for your own task, and why. Scoring, which comes next, gives you a fair way to compare it with the others.

title.text: Score every risk as likelihood times impact

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_matrix_7.70x4.80_0414f65c.png
objects.alt: Score every risk as likelihood times impact

objects.text: Likelihood times impact gives a score from 1 to 25.

runs.text: High is 15 or more. Medium is 8 to 14. Low is below 8.
High needs a control and a report to the Managing Director.
Positions here are illustrative.

slides.notes:
This picture sorts risks. Across is how likely a risk is in the next twelve months, from one to five. Up is how bad it would be, from one to five. Multiply the two. The score puts the risk in a band, the same bands as the Scale sheet in your Risk Register.

Fifteen or more is High: it needs a control, and the owner reports it to the Managing Director. Eight to fourteen is Medium: a control and a review date. Below eight is Low: accept it and watch. The positions here are illustrative, and yours will differ because your task is different.

title.text:
Four responses to a risk:
reduce, share, accept or avoid

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_icons_7.70x4.80_6407e0f2.png
objects.alt: Four responses to a risk: reduce, share, accept or avoid

objects.text: Every scored risk gets one of these four.

runs.text: Most risks end in reduce.
Low risks are often accepted.
A High risk you accept needs a reason you can defend.

slides.notes:
Once a risk has a score, you choose a response, and there are four. Reduce: add a control and a named owner. Most risks end here. Share: move part of the risk to a supplier contract or to insurance. Accept: record the risk, watch it and set a date to review it.

That suits a Low risk. Avoid: stop that use of AI until a control exists. If you accept a High risk, you need a reason you could defend to the owner of the business. Keep these four words, because you use them in your decision at the end of the session.

Use it as a checklist for your own work.
The AI management standard. Auditors can certify it.
Ask a vendor which standard it holds.

A continental strategy for national plans.
Watch for national rules that follow it.

Its staff-training duty is a model.

slides.notes:
Six names you will hear. NIST is a voluntary framework from the United States with four functions: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. Use it as a checklist. ISO forty-two thousand and one is the AI management standard, and an auditor can certify it. In my experience, most vendors hold SOC 2 or ISO 27001, which are security standards, so when a vendor says certified, ask which standard and ask to see the report.

The OECD principles are shared values. The African Union has a continental strategy. The EU AI Act applies only if you serve customers in the EU. The Uganda strategy can change, so I re-check it the week we meet.

title.text:
Uganda has no AI statute, and the
2019 Data Protection Act applies

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_icons_7.70x4.80_08ca4c9b.png
objects.alt: Uganda has no AI statute, and the 2019 Data Protection Act applies

objects.text: The Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019 applies to personal data.

runs.text: Check your duties, including whether and when to report a breach, with your lawyer or the Personal Data Protection Office.

slides.notes:
Uganda has no law written only for AI. That does not mean no rules. My understanding is that the Data Protection and Privacy Act 2019 applies to personal data, including when it is used with an AI tool. The three columns show the position: no AI statute, the 2019 Act, and your own policy filling the gap.

I am not a lawyer, and this is not legal advice. For your duties, such as registration, sending data abroad and reporting a breach, confirm with your lawyer or the Personal Data Protection Office. If you ask me, I will give you my understanding and send you to them.

slides.notes:
Five questions to take to your lawyer or to the Personal Data Protection Office. I do not answer them for you, because the detail depends on your company and the law can change. Which of our AI uses involve personal data?

What are our duties under the 2019 Act for each use?

Whether and when must we report a breach?

What must a vendor contract say about our data?

And what must we tell staff and customers?

Until you have the answers, keep personal data such as CVs and customer lists out of free tools.

title.text:
A ban can push AI use out
of sight, so write a policy

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_cross_0.75.png

objects.text: Ban only

runs.text: Staff may still use personal accounts.
You cannot see what data leaves.
Nobody is trained or checked.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_shield_0.75.png

objects.text: Policy and approved tools

runs.text: Company accounts with a named owner.
Data rules by sensitivity.
Training and one place to report.

objects.text: Shadow AI is staff using AI through personal accounts. A policy gives them a safe route.

slides.notes:
Many executives ask whether to ban AI. In my experience, and in what many companies report, a ban pushes use out of sight. People use personal accounts anyway, which is called shadow AI. Then you cannot see what data leaves, and nobody is trained. A policy gives staff a safe route: company accounts with a named owner, clear rules on what data may go in, training, and one place to report a problem.

Nile Valley Foods already has a handbook rule against pasting customer data into a public AI tool without written approval. A policy extends that rule and gives staff something they may use.

title.text:
When something goes
wrong: five steps, then fix it

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_b18020bb.png
objects.alt: When something goes wrong: five steps, then fix it

objects.text: Then fix the cause, test again and update the policy. The NVF handbook asks for a suspected data loss to be reported within 4 hours.

slides.notes:
If something goes wrong, there are five steps and then the fix. Stop or switch off, using the off switch you built in Session 8. Tell the owner of the automation at once, and never blame someone for reporting in good faith. Do the task by hand with the old method, so the work still gets done.

Record what happened, when and which data was involved. Decide who must be told: customers, staff and, if personal data leaked, whether and when to report to the Personal Data Protection Office. Ask your lawyer or the Office, and do not guess. Then fix the cause, test again and update the policy.

title.text:
Demonstration: rank sample
CVs with and without names

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_7.30x3.90_0bba851d.png
objects.alt: Demonstration: rank sample CVs with and without names

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: Does the order change?
Does any reason use something the job does not need?
Who answers for the result?

slides.notes:
Now a bias demonstration with synthetic CVs, so no real person is involved. The three steps on the left show the plan. I give an AI tool three sample CVs and the job description for a dispatch clerk and ask for a ranking with reasons. Then I remove names, home areas and school names and ask again.

I do not know in advance what the tool will say, so we check the live result together. Watch whether the order changes and whether a reason uses something the job does not need. Names can point to a region, a gender or a background, and a tool can repeat that without warning.

We began with this question: What could go wrong, and what rules should my company set? Before you go, say in one sentence what you can now say about it.
